In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
glial calcium signaling is a critical regulator of neuronal excitability.
glia regulate neuronal excitability through a novel mechanism of endocytosis of K+ channel proteins, and that this process is controlled by glial calcium levels.
glial Ca2+-dependent endocytosis regulates neuronal excitability through the modulation of K+ buffering around the soma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
glial endocytic dysfunction leads to a reduction in K2P channel expression on glial cell membrane, which in turn causes an imbalance of K+ homeostasis and leads to neuronal hyperexcitability.
glia can regulate neuronal activity via a novel mechanism of K+ buffering that is independent of the classical role of K+ buffering at the synaptic cleft.
we show that glia regulate neuronal excitability by controlling the expression of K+ channels at neuronal soma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
glial Ca2+, which is known to be important in glial-neuronal interactions at synapses, also regulates neuronal excitability by controlling endocytic trafficking of a K2P ion channel.
glia can influence neuronal excitability by regulating the activity of K2P channels in the soma.
we show a novel link between glial calcium and neuronal excitability, specifically through a glial K+ channel that regulates the excitability of the neurons that it surrounds.
